citation.title: Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment

standing_assumptions:
[Population and design: pp. 1914–1915 (PDF pp. 3–4)] Formally, suppose we have a finite population $U$ of units indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$ on which a randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, M\}$ specifies which of $M$ possible treatment values that unit $i$ receives. An experimental design contains a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ from the $M^N$ different possibilities with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by a given experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$ so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Our analysis below focuses on the case where the design is known in the following sense: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ for all $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ is known. [Exposure mapping: p. 1915 (PDF p. 4)] We define an exposure mapping as a function that maps an assignment vector and unit-specific traits to an exposure value: $f : \Omega 	imes \Theta 	o \Delta$, where $	heta_i \in \Theta$ quantifies relevant traits of unit $i$. [Exposures and exposure probabilities: p. 1916 (PDF p. 5)] Define the exposure that unit $i$ receives as $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z}, 	heta_i)$, a random variable with support $\Delta_i \subseteq \Delta$ and for which $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. Note that because $|\Delta| \le |\Omega| 	imes N$, $\Delta$ is a finite set of $K \le |\Omega| 	imes N$ values, such that $\Delta = \{d_1, \ldots, d_K\}$. Then for each unit, $i$, we have a vector of probabilities, $(\pi_i(d_1), \ldots, \pi_i(d_K))' =  oldsymbol{\pi}_i$. [...] We have $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)$. [...] we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$ as the probability of the joint event that both units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposure $d_k$, and we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ as the probability of the joint event that units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposures $d_k$ and $d_l$, respectively. [Probability matrices: p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ is an $N 	imes N$ symmetric matrix with individual exposure probabilities, the $\pi_i(d_k)$'s, on the diagonal and joint exposure probabilities, the $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$'s, on the off-diagonals. The nonsymmetric $N 	imes N$ matrix $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$, with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$, yields all joint probabilities across exposure conditions $k$ and $l$. The zeroes on the diagonal are due to the fact that a unit cannot be subject to multiple exposure conditions at once. [Positivity: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] Suppose all units have nonzero probabilities of being subject to each of the $K$ exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and $k$. [Potential outcomes: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] In the most general terms, each $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ can generate a potential outcome for unit $i$. We label the randomization potential outcome of unit $i$ associated with $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$. These randomization potential outcomes are fixed for all units in the population and do not depend on the value of randomized treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$. CONDITION 1 (Properly specified exposure mapping). For all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', 	heta_i)$, $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Given Condition 1, each unit $i$ has $|\Delta| = K$ potential outcomes, which we can write in terms of the exposure conditions as $(y_i(d_1), \ldots, y_i(d_K))$, where $y_i(d_k) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, and $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k$. Let $Y_i$ be the observed outcome for unit $i$. CONDITION 2 (Consistent potential outcomes). $Y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) y_i(d_k)$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. [p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] Throughout, unless otherwise noted, we will be assuming Conditions 1 and 2. [Estimands: p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] We seek estimates for all $k$ of $\mu(d_k) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) =  rac{1}{N} y^T(d_k)$, where $y^T(d_k)$ is the total of the potential outcomes under $d_k$. This allows us to define an average causal effect of being in exposure condition $d_k$ as compared to being in condition $d_l$ as $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) -  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_l)$. [Estimators: pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] (1) $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}$. $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) = (1/N)\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) = (1/N^2)\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. (3) $\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_l) =  rac{1}{N}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$, which is an estimator of $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]$, the average unit-level causal effect of exposure $k$ versus exposure $l$. [Exact probabilities: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9)] from here on our analysis assumes that we are working with $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ and $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$ [the exact exposure probabilities; the simulated probabilities $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ enter only Propositions 3.1 and 4.1]. [Variance and covariance estimators of Section 5, used by several targets: pp. 1921–1924 (PDF pp. 10–13)] Given $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, the Horvitz–Thompson estimator for $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is (7) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i \in U} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)[1 - \pi_i(d_k)] \left[ rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}ight]^2 + \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) 	imes  rac{\pi_{ij}(d_k) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_k)}$. [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] (This notation requires that we define $0/0 = 0$.) [p. 1922] $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_k)}ight]$, noting that $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = 0$ if $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$. [p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] For the case where $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$, we propose the Horvitz–Thompson-type estimator for the covariance (8) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_l) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] a more general estimator for the covariance (10) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924] we obtain a conservative variance estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l))$ as (11) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] =  rac{1}{N^2}\{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_l) - 2\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]\}$. [Asymptotic framework and the conditions of Section 6. These are not standing assumptions: they are transcribed here once because several targets invoke them, and a target carries one of them only where its statement names it.] [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] Consider a sequence of nested populations indexed by size $N$, $(U_N)$. To define a notion of asymptotic growth, we let $N$ tend to infinity, allowing for the experimental design to be reapplied anew to each $U_N$, subject to the conditions defined below. [p. 1925 (PDF p. 14)] CONDITION 3 (Boundedness of potential outcomes and exposure probabilities). Potential outcomes and exposure probabilities are bounded so that, for all values $i$ and $d_k$, $|y_i(d_k)| \le c_1 < \infty$ and $|1/\pi_i(d_k)| \le c_2 < \infty$. There exists a finite constant $m$ such that, for all $U_N$, $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$. [p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] CONDITION 6 (Nonzero limiting variance.). $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} c$, where $c > 0$. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are taken over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$ with weights $p_{\mathbf{z}}$; the population, the traits $	heta_i$, the exposure mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. $U \setminus i$ means $U \setminus \{i\}$. Each unit receives exactly one exposure, so $\sum_{k} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) = 1$, $\pi_{ii}(d_k) = \pi_i(d_k)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d_k, d_l) = 0$ for $d_k

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 9, the two descriptions of the simulation design's exposure probabilities (the degree-39 student; no no-exposure probability below 0.01), corrected claim
canonical_claim.location: p. 1931 (PDF p. 20); design and exposure mapping on p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements: p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)] We simulate experiments in which a treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$, is randomly assigned without replacement and with uniform probability to 1/10 of individuals in a school network. [p. 1931 (PDF p. 20)] [...] with a maximum degree of 39. To give an idea of the range of exposure probabilities, for the student with degree of 39, the probability of isolated direct exposure was 0.00067. [...] About 3% of students have an exposure probability of less than 0.01 for the direct + indirect exposure condition, 0.5% for isolated direct exposure, and then there were no cases with probabilities less than 0.01 for either the indirect- or no-exposure conditions. [Corrected claim, from the validator] Read as probabilities under the stated design, the value 0.00067 for the degree-39 student and the statement that no student has a no-exposure probability below 0.01 are incompatible: at least one of them is inaccurate as a description of design probabilities (they can both hold for finite Monte Carlo estimates of the probabilities, which the section does not say it reports). Which one is inaccurate, and its corrected value, cannot be determined without the school's size and number treated. [Formal content] Let a school have $N$ subjects of whom exactly $n$ are treated, every set of $n$ subjects being equally likely, and let subject $i$ have 39 neighbours in the school, with $1 \le n \le N - 39$. Let $p = \pi_i(d_{10})$ be the probability that $i$ is treated and none of its neighbours is, and $q = \pi_i(d_{00})$ the probability that neither $i$ nor any of its neighbours is treated. (a) $p = \binom{N - 40}{n - 1}\big/\binom{N}{n}$ and $q = \binom{N - 40}{n}\big/\binom{N}{n}$. (b) $q = \frac{N - 39 - n}{n}\,p$. (c) If $N \le 10n + 5$ (which holds when $n = N/10$ and when $n$ is $N/10$ rounded to the nearest integer), then $q \le 9p$. (d) Hence, under (c), $p \le 0.000675$ (every value that rounds to 0.00067 at five decimals satisfies this) implies $q \le 243/40000 = 0.006075 < 0.01$; and $q \ge 1/100$ implies $p \ge 1/900 > 0.000675$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Exposure mapping of Section 9: p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)] $\theta_i$ is a column vector equal to the transpose of subject $i$'s row in a network adjacency matrix (modified such that we have zeroes on the diagonal). The inner product, $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$, counts the number of subject $i$'s peers assigned to treatment. $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_{11}$ (Direct + Indirect Exposure) if $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$; $d_{10}$ (Isolated Direct Exposure) if $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$; $d_{01}$ (Indirect Exposure) if $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$; $d_{00}$ (No Exposure) if $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$, where each unit falls into exactly one of the four exposure conditions. Here $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. [p. 1930] Indirect effects are transmitted only within a subject's school. [p. 1931 (PDF p. 20)] This experiment is repeated independently across the 144 school classes included in Add Health [...]. $\pi_i(d)$ is the exposure probability of the standing assumptions, computed for the design within subject $i$'s school.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For $1 \le n \le N - 40$, $\binom{N-40}{n}\big/\binom{N-40}{n-1} = \frac{N - 39 - n}{n}$; for $n = N - 39$, $q = 0$ and (b) holds with both sides zero. $N \le 10n + 5$ gives $\frac{N - 39 - n}{n} \le 9 - \frac{34}{n} < 9$.
canonical_claim.note: P013-N004 is rated an error, Minor (verdict confirmed in part). Like P013-T10 it is a finding about reported numbers whose content is an exact incompatibility; no corrected number can be supplied from the paper. The validator holds a Lean algebraic certificate of (c) and (d) taking (b) as a hypothesis (validate/P013-N004/v1/artifact/check.lean), and derives (a) and (b) by counting; (a) and (b) are the part still to be formalized on a finite probability space. The bound $q < 9p$ also holds when $n$ is $N/10$ rounded down or up, since then $N < 10n + 10 \le 10n + 39$. Not established: which statement is inaccurate; that the published numbers are Monte Carlo estimates (the staged later script uses 1,500 draws, and $1/1501$ rounds to 0.00067); any effect on Table 1.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9); proof in Appendix A.3, p. 1938 (PDF p. 27)
canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, p. 1920 (PDF p. 9)] PROPOSITION 4.1. The relative bias for $\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)$ is bounded as $\left|\frac{\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] - y^T(d_k)}{y^T(d_k)}\right| \le (1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}$, where $\pi_0(d_k) = \min_i\{\pi_i(d_k)\}$. [Rule drawn from it, p. 1920] For a relative bias target of $b$ and given some approximation of $\pi_0(d_k)$, the bound implies selecting a number of replicates $R \ge \log(b)/\log(1 - \pi_0(d_k)) - 1$. Thus, for $b = 0.005$ and $\pi_0(d_k) = 0.0005$, this would imply at least 10,593 replicates. [No hypothesis is attached beyond the setting: Conditions 1 and 2, $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$, and replicates drawn from the randomization plan. No sign condition on the potential outcomes and no condition $y^T(d_k) \ne 0$ is stated.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] One may nonetheless approximate the $\boldsymbol{\pi}_i$'s and joint probabilities with arbitrary precision through simulation, that is, produce $R$ random replicate $\mathbf{z}$'s based on the randomization plan. [pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] Above we indicated that one can approximate $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ with $(\hat{\mathbf{I}}_k\hat{\mathbf{I}}_k' + \iota_N)/(R + 1)$, which has diagonal elements, $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k) = \frac{X_i + 1}{R + 1}$, where $X_i = \sum_{r=1}^{R} \mathbf{I}_r(f(\mathbf{z}_r, \theta_i) = d_k)$ and $r = 1, \ldots, R$ indexes the replicates. Define the Horvitz–Thompson estimator that uses the $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ estimates: $\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{Y_i}{\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)}$. [Proof as printed, Appendix A.3, p. 1938 (PDF p. 27)] We have $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)\pi_i(d_k)\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R+1}{X_i+1}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)[1 - (1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}] = y^T(d_k) - \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)(1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}$. And so $|\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] - y^T(d_k)| = \left|\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)(1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}\right| \le |y^T(d_k)|(1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}$.
canonical_claim.note: False as printed for potential outcomes of mixed sign, and undefined when $y^T(d_k) = 0$: counterexample P013-T3, corrected statement P013-T4. The equalities of Appendix A.3 are correct for independent replicates; only its last inequality fails. The sentence introducing the proposition prints the target as $\widehat{y^T}(d_k)$; it is $y^T(d_k)$ (P013-T9). The numerical example (10,593) is correct.

canonical_claim.statement: [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] LEMMA 5.1. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. PROPOSITION 5.1. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0$ for some $i, j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + A$, where $A = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} y_i(d_k)y_j(d_k)$. PROPOSITION 5.2. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k)] \ge \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. [Hypotheses: the standing assumptions (a known design, Conditions 1 and 2, $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$) and the convention $0/0 = 0$ in expression (7); Proposition 5.2 carries no further condition and covers both cases.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Expression (7), the convention $0/0 = 0$ and $\widehat{A_2}(d_k)$ are in the standing assumptions (pp. 1921–1922). $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is given by expression (2) (P013-T13). [The general sampling results the paper reproduces, Appendix A.5, pp. 1939–1942 (PDF pp. 28–31), for a population $U$ indexed by $k$ with inclusion indicators $I_k$, $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k > 0$, $\mathrm{E}(I_kI_l) = \pi_{kl}$ and $\hat{t} = \sum_{k \in U} I_k y_k/\pi_k$] PROPOSITION A.1. When $s^0$ refers to a sample from a design with some $\pi_{kl} = 0$, we have $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{t})] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t}) + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U \setminus k : \pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_ky_l = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t}) + A$. [Here, as its proof on p. 1940 writes it for such a design, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{t}) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U : \pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_kI_l \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$.] Now, consider the following variance estimator: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_C}(\hat{t}) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U : \pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_kI_l \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U \setminus k : \pi_{kl} = 0\}} \left(I_k\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}\pi_k} + I_l\frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}\pi_l}\right)$, where $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ are positive real numbers such that $\frac{1}{a_{kl}} + \frac{1}{b_{kl}} = 1$ for all pairs $k, l$ with $\pi_{kl} = 0$. PROPOSITION A.2. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_C}(\hat{t})] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t})$. COROLLARY A.2 [the case $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$, estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_{C2}}(\hat{t})$]. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_{C2}}(\hat{t})] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t})$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-population statements; both readers verified them by exact enumeration on designs with zero joint probabilities and mixed-sign outcomes, and no error touches them. They apply the sampling results of Appendix A.5 with inclusion indicator $\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)$ and value $y_i(d_k)$. With $0/0 = 0$, a pair with $\pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0$ contributes nothing to (7). The inequality behind Proposition 5.2 is Young's inequality with exponents 2: $y_i(d_k)^2/2 + y_j(d_k)^2/2 \ge |y_i(d_k)||y_j(d_k)| \ge -y_i(d_k)y_j(d_k)$, so $A + \mathrm{E}[\widehat{A_2}(d_k)] \ge 0$. The paper also states (p. 1922) that an unbiased estimator for the variance of $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)$ is $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)] = (1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ under the condition of Lemma 5.1, and defines $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_A}[\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)] = (1/N^2) [\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k)]$.
